section.title: The Fool Says There Is No God
section.sectionRationale: A wisdom lament diagnosing the universal condition of humanity apart from God, later quoted at length by Paul in Romans 3 as scriptural proof that none are righteous. It closes Book I's cluster of laments with a longing look toward the salvation of Israel, and stands as one of the Bible's clearest short statements of total human corruption and hoped for restoration.
section.thesis: Apart from God, humanity's corruption is universal and total, yet even here the psalm does not end in despair but reaches for the salvation that will come from Zion.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the fool's denial and the universal corruption it reveals; the oppression of God's people by workers of iniquity; and the longing cry for salvation from Zion.

units.label: There is no one who does good
units.note: the fool's denial and universal corruption

verses.text:
The {{nabal|fool}} says in his heart, “There is no God.” 
They are corrupt; their acts are vile. There is no one who does good.
The LORD looks down from heaven upon the sons of men to see if any understand, if any seek God.
All have turned away, they have together become corrupt; there is no one who does good, not even one.

units.label: They devour my people like bread

verses.text:
Will the workers of iniquity never learn? 
They devour my people like bread; they refuse to call upon the LORD.
There they are, overwhelmed with dread, for God is in the company of the righteous.
You sinners frustrate the plans of the oppressed, yet the LORD is their {{machaseh|shelter}}.

units.label: Let Jacob rejoice
units.note: the longing for salvation from Zion

verses.text:
Oh, that the {{yeshuah|salvation}} of Israel would come from Zion! 
When the LORD restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!

nabal.gloss: Fool, one morally and spiritually senseless, not merely intellectually deficient. In Hebrew thought the fool's denial of God is a matter of the heart and will, a practical atheism lived out in corrupt action rather than a reasoned philosophical position.

machaseh.gloss: Shelter, refuge, a place of protection from storm or attack. Even while sinners frustrate the plans of the oppressed, the psalm insists the LORD Himself remains their machaseh, their true and sufficient hiding place.

yeshuah.gloss: Salvation, deliverance, rescue. The psalmist longs for this yeshuah to come out of Zion for all Israel, the same word later given as the personal name of Jesus, the one through whom that salvation finally comes.

basic.context: The psalm opens with the fool's quiet, practical denial, 'There is no God', spoken in his heart, and moves at once to describe the corruption that follows from it. God looks down and finds no one who does good, not even one. That corruption then turns predatory, oppressing God's people, who have nowhere else to turn but to the LORD as their shelter. The psalm ends with a longing prayer that salvation would come from Zion and restore God's people to joy.
basic.hermeneutics: This is not a psalm about a few obviously wicked people out there; verses 2-3 describe the human race as a whole, apart from God's grace, which is exactly how Paul later uses it in Romans 3 to prove that every person, Jew and Gentile alike, stands guilty before God. The psalm both diagnoses the disease and points, in its final verse, toward the only cure.
basic.originalLanguages: The nabal, fool, denies God not as an intellectual argument but as a practical stance of the heart, lived out in corrupt action. Even under oppression the LORD remains machaseh, shelter, for the righteous, and the psalm's closing hope is that yeshuah, salvation, the very word behind the name Jesus, would come from Zion.
basic.typology: Zion, the place from which salvation is longed for here, points forward to the greater Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Christ Himself, who brings the salvation this psalm can only long for and name, but not yet see.
basic.christ: Paul quotes this psalm in Romans 3:10-12 as part of his case that all have sinned and no one is righteous, precisely so that he can then present Christ as the only remedy, the righteousness of God given through faith in Jesus to all who believe, apart from human merit.
basic.god: God is shown searching, looking down from heaven to see if anyone understands or seeks Him, revealing both His patience and the depth of the problem He finds. Yet He is also shelter for the oppressed and the one from whom true salvation will come.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3:10-12 quotes this psalm directly as scriptural proof of universal sin. Psalm 53 repeats this psalm nearly word for word with small variations. Isaiah 59:2 shows the same theme, that sin separates humanity from God.
basic.oneStory: This psalm names humanity's universal condition apart from grace and then reaches, in its very last breath, for the salvation that must come from outside that condition, from Zion, a longing finally answered when salvation came from Zion in the person of Jesus Christ.

context.literary:
Psalm 14 is built like a courtroom scene with three movements of unequal length. Verses 1 to 3 are the indictment, and they are shaped as a descent: a single fool speaking privately in verse 1, then 'the sons of men' inspected from heaven in verse 2, then 'all' in verse 3. The scope widens from one voice to the whole race, and the phrase 'there is no one who does good' appears at the end of verse 1 and again, sharpened by 'not even one', at the end of verse 3. That repetition is the frame of the whole diagnosis.

The middle movement, verses 4 to 6, turns from accusation to the victims. It opens with a rhetorical question, 'Will the workers of iniquity never learn?', and moves into a compact scene of sudden terror, 'There they are, overwhelmed with dread.' The word 'there' points a finger, as though the psalmist can see the moment of reversal. Three names for the wronged crowd the section: 'my people' in verse 4, 'the righteous' in verse 5, and 'the oppressed' in verse 6. Set against them are the fool of verse 1 and the 'workers of iniquity' of verse 4. The psalm thus holds two pictures side by side, a universal corruption and a specific class of predators, and does not pretend they fit neatly together.

Verse 7 is a short cry with a change of mood. The accusation has ended; what remains is longing. The psalm runs from a fool's silent thought in verse 1 to a whole people's hope in verse 7, and it ends where the fool began, in the heart, but now with God as its object.

The psalm has a twin in Psalm 53, which repeats it with small changes. In Psalm 14 God is 'the LORD', the covenant name, while Psalm 53 uses the general word 'God' throughout, in keeping with the collection of psalms in which it sits. The largest difference is in verse 5, where Psalm 53:5 speaks of God scattering 'the bones of those who besieged you.' The Psalter therefore preserves the poem twice, a reminder that Israel sang and edited its psalms for different settings in worship.
context.historical:
The title, 'For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David,' places the psalm in David's court and in the worship he organised around the ark. Two facts from David's own story give the psalm its edge. The first is the man Nabal, whose name means 'fool,' and of whom his own servant said, 'His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him,' 1 Samuel 25:25. David nearly killed his household in anger at his contempt, and learned how a fool speaks and acts when he thinks no one holds him to account. The second is Zion, the fortress David captured from the Jebusites, 2 Samuel 5:6-9, and to which he brought the ark. From that point on, Zion was where the LORD was understood to dwell among His people, Psalm 9:11, and the place from which help was expected, Psalm 20:2.

The word 'fool' in the Bible describes a moral condition, and the psalm's hearers would not have taken it as a philosophical position. The fool does not calculate that God is absent; he lives as though nobody stands over him. Israel's neighbours were polytheists, so open atheism as we now know it hardly existed in the ancient world, and the psalm is aimed at something more common: the person who lives, rules, lends and judges as though no divine witness were watching. Psalm 10:4 and Psalm 10:11 describe the same attitude.

The last verse speaks of a people restored from captivity. A psalm ascribed to David could mean this in a general way, as a picture of God turning the fortunes of His people, an idiom also used of Job, Job 42:10. Other readers think a later editor has adjusted the last verse for the exile, when the phrase would be literal. The psalm's oppressors, who 'devour my people like bread,' fit the era of David's enemies and equally the times of the prophets, when the powerful did the same to the poor, as in Micah 3:3 and Isaiah 3:14-15.
context.canonical:
Psalm 14 is the great Old Testament statement of universal sin, and it is taken up by the New Testament in a way that few passages are. In Romans 3:9-18 Paul builds a chain of quotations to prove that 'Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin,' beginning with a free quotation of Psalm 14:1-3, 'There is no one righteous, not even one. There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God,' Romans 3:10-11. He then adds lines from Psalm 5:9, Psalm 140:3, Psalm 10:7, Isaiah 59:7-8 and Psalm 36:1, so that the psalm becomes the head of a longer indictment. He also draws on Psalm 143:2, 'no one alive is righteous before You,' to make the same point in Romans 3:20, and on Ecclesiastes 7:20, which says there is 'no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.'

The psalm also looks back. 'The LORD looks down from heaven upon the sons of men' recalls Genesis 6:12, where God looked at the earth and saw that it 'was corrupt,' and Genesis 11:5, where He 'came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of men were building.' In each case the LORD inspects human beings and finds them wanting. Psalm 14 states what those stories illustrate.

Then it looks forward. The final prayer, 'Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion,' is the hope that runs through the prophets and is picked up in Romans 11:26, 'The Deliverer will come from Zion,' a quotation modelled on Isaiah 59:20, which itself speaks of a Redeemer coming to Zion. And Hebrews 12:22 announces to believers, 'you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.' The longing of Psalm 14:7 becomes the confession of the church.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist meant his hearers to stop treating wickedness as somebody else's problem. The psalm begins by naming a fool, and the first hearers, quick to agree that fools exist, would have nodded. Then verse 2 lifts the lens and the finding is that God looks and sees no exception. The point is not to make people despair but to bring them to the place where verse 7 makes sense: a rescue has to come from outside, and it has to come from God.

He also meant to comfort. The middle of the psalm is directed at the poor and the wronged, telling them that God is 'in the company of the righteous' and that He is their shelter, verses 5 and 6. Those who were being eaten like bread were to learn that their oppressors were the ones who ought to be afraid. And he meant his people to pray. The psalm does not end with a lecture on sin, but with a longing that God would come and restore. First hearers were meant to leave the sanctuary with an honest view of the human race, with trust in a God who sees, and with a prayer on their lips for salvation from Zion.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes what God finds when He looks, and it does not tell anyone to practise corruption or to treat others as corrupt. Its generalisations about humanity are a verdict on the race, not permission to write off any person we happen to meet. It also describes the oppression of God's people without prescribing how they must respond to it beyond taking refuge in the LORD and praying for salvation.

The application is that no one is entitled to stand above the psalm. It is a mirror before it is a weapon, and Paul's use of it in Romans 3 is aimed at closing every mouth, Romans 3:19, including the mouths of the religious. The psalm also teaches that comfort belongs to the wronged, and that the faithful may wait for God to act rather than take the law into their own hands. It should not be used to justify contempt for unbelievers, since the same Scripture that says 'no one does good' says that God has sought the lost, as Titus 3:3-5 describes: 'at one time we too were foolish,' yet God our Savior saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done.

debates.question: Is the fool's 'There is no God' a theory or a way of living?

views.label: Practical atheism: a life lived as if God were not there
views.case: The fool 'says in his heart', which is the place of intention as well as thought, and what follows is not an argument but a list of deeds, corruption and vile acts. Psalm 10:4 and Psalm 10:11 describe the same posture, 'in all his schemes there is no God' and 'He says to himself, God has forgotten.' Most interpreters take it this way, and the ancient world had few theoretical atheists.

views.label: An actual denial of God's existence or of His involvement
views.case: Some hold that the words mean what they say: the fool concludes there is no God, or none who acts among human beings. The psalm's sarcasm carries more sting if the fool does hold the opinion, and Paul in Romans 1:20-22 speaks of those who suppress the truth and become fools.

debates.bearing: Both readings arrive at the same place. What the psalm condemns is a heart that removes God from the picture, and it treats moral corruption as the fruit of that removal, whether the removal is a doctrine or a habit.

debates.question: Does 'no one who does good' include the righteous of verse 5?

views.label: It is a sweeping statement about humanity apart from grace, and the righteous are those God has made so
views.case: Paul applies this very language in Romans 3 to the whole race, Jew and Gentile, while elsewhere describing believers as righteous by faith, Romans 3:22. On this reading the 'righteous' of verse 5 are righteous because they take refuge in the LORD, not because they never sin.

views.label: It describes a particular class of persecutors in Israel, in contrast to the faithful
views.case: Verses 4 to 6 speak of 'my people' and 'the righteous' as distinct from the workers of iniquity who devour them, which suggests to some that the harshest language falls on a specific corrupt group and that the poem does not describe every person.

debates.bearing: The psalm sets both facts in view, that corruption is universal and that God has a people who are His. Paul's reading in Romans 3 does not cancel the second, it explains how a sinner becomes one of them: 'through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe,' Romans 3:22.

debates.question: What is the 'captivity' that God restores in verse 7?

views.label: The exile in Babylon, so the verse comes from a later hand
views.case: The phrase is most often used of return from exile, as in Psalm 85:1 and Psalm 126:1, and the psalm's final verse would be at home in the time of the return.

views.label: A general reversal of fortunes, which need not mean exile
views.case: The same idiom is used of Job when God 'restored his prosperity,' Job 42:10, where no captivity is in view, so David could speak of God turning his people's distress around without any exile in sight.

debates.bearing: Either way the psalm ends by hoping for God's own rescue from Zion, and the Christian reader sees that hope completed in Christ, who releases captives of every kind, Luke 4:18.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening verse says that the fool speaks 'in his heart.' In Hebrew thought the heart is not only the place of feeling but of thought and will, so to say something 'in the heart' is to set a course. The same idiom appears in Psalm 10:6 and Psalm 10:11, where the wicked man says to himself that nothing will shake him and that God does not see. The phrase 'There is no God' is literally 'no God', without a verb, which lets it be taken as 'no God for me', 'no God here', or 'no God who matters.'

Next, the fool's deeds are 'corrupt' and 'vile.' The verb for corrupt is the same verb the flood story uses when God saw that the earth 'was corrupt', Genesis 6:12, and it carries the sense of spoiling something that was made good. The word for 'vile' is built on the root that gives the Old Testament's word for what God abhors, and the word for 'acts' is a general one for deeds and doings; it is used for God's deeds too, in Psalm 9:11. The fool has been busy, and what he has been doing has turned the world's good things sour.

Verse 2 asks whether anyone 'understands' and 'seeks God.' The first verb is the one from which the word maskil, a wise or skilled person, is formed; the second is the ordinary verb for seeking out, inquiring after, and it is the word behind Psalm 24:6, 'the generation of those who seek Him.' The pairing covers mind and will: no one thinks straight about God, and no one goes after Him. This is why Paul can quote it as evidence of universal sin in Romans 3:11.

The Greek Bible adds something. Many manuscripts of the Septuagint of this psalm carry a run of extra lines after verse 3, about throats like open graves and the venom of vipers, matching the chain Paul assembles in Romans 3:13-18. Most scholars think those lines were brought into the Greek psalm from other passages, Psalm 5:9, Psalm 140:3, Psalm 10:7 and Isaiah 59:7-8, though whether Paul found them there or built the chain himself is debated. Either way, the Hebrew text of Psalm 14 has no such lines, and the BSB translates the Hebrew.

In verse 5 the Hebrew is 'they feared a great fear', with the verb and its own noun side by side to intensify it. The BSB's 'overwhelmed with dread' catches the force. The word 'there' before it makes it a scene that can be pointed at.

The last verse begins with a common Hebrew wish, literally 'Who will give?', translated 'Oh, that.' It is the same exclamation Moses uses in Deuteronomy 5:29, 'If only they had such a heart.' It expresses longing that stretches out for something the speaker cannot produce. The phrase for restoring the 'captive people' turns on a verb of returning and a noun for captivity, and it is an idiom that can also mean turning fortunes around, as in Job 42:10.

typology.fulfillment: David's Zion was the fortress where the ark rested and from which the LORD was expected to help His people, Psalm 20:2. The psalm's last verse looks to a salvation still to come 'from Zion.' The New Testament says believers 'have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' Hebrews 12:22, where Jesus is the mediator of a new covenant, Hebrews 12:24. The earthly hill was a pointer; the place where God's people are gathered to Him is in Christ. The type falls short because Jerusalem could be attacked, while the city Hebrews describes is unshakable, Hebrews 12:28.

typology.type: The LORD who looks down to see
typology.fulfillment: The psalm has God look down from heaven and find no one who seeks Him. The story of Babel says He 'came down to see,' Genesis 11:5, and the search in Psalm 14 finds its answer when He comes down in person. 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and 'the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10. Where the psalm says none seek God, the gospel says God seeks. The correspondence is between a God who looks and a God who comes; it is exceeded because in Christ He does not only see the trouble but enters it.

typology.type: The oppressed people, devoured like bread
typology.fulfillment: The psalm's poor are those whom the wicked 'devour ... like bread.' Christ identifies Himself with such people. When Saul persecuted the church, the risen Lord said, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?' Acts 9:4, and He tells the nations that what they did to the least of His brothers they did to Him, Matthew 25:40. He is also the one who became poor for our sake, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and the 'bread of life,' John 6:35, who gives Himself to be eaten rather than devouring anyone. The pattern is a real correspondence, though the psalm says only that God is with the righteous, while in Christ God shares their suffering.

The final hope is that the LORD will restore His captive people. Christ opens His ministry by quoting Isaiah, 'He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives ... to release the oppressed,' Luke 4:18, and the release He brings reaches beyond exile to sin and death. The correspondence is the pattern of God reversing a captivity; the escalation is that the captivity is now the bondage of sin, and the type falls short because a return to the land could not finish the work, while the return that Christ brings ends in a place no enemy can enter.

study.christ:
Psalm 14 leads to Christ mainly by contrast and by longing, and its most important New Testament use is a diagnostic one. Paul quotes it in Romans 3:10-12 so that every mouth may be silenced and 'the whole world held accountable to God,' Romans 3:19, and then he turns the page: 'But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed ... through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe,' Romans 3:21-22. The psalm is the dark ground against which that light shines. Paul does not treat Psalm 14 as a prediction of the Messiah. He treats it as an accurate description of the human race, which the gospel then answers.

There is, however, a striking exception that the psalm's universality throws into relief. 'There is no one who does good, not even one.' Jesus does not exempt Himself from that verdict by being one more good man. He says, 'Why do you call Me good? No one is good except God alone,' Mark 10:18, a saying that reads as an invitation to see who He is rather than a denial of His goodness. Hebrews describes Him as 'one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15, and Paul says that God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. The Bible is not describing a good person who slipped past the psalm's net, but God Himself in human form entering a race the psalm has declared corrupt.

The search of verse 2 finds its answer in Christ. In the psalm, God looks down from heaven and finds no one seeking Him. In the gospel, 'the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10. Here the movement reverses: since no one seeks God, God seeks. Isaiah says the same in a related setting, 'The LORD looked and was displeased that there was no justice. He saw that there was no man ... So His own arm brought salvation,' Isaiah 59:15-16, and the next verses promise a Redeemer for Zion, Isaiah 59:20, which Paul takes up in Romans 11:26.

The 'my people' of verses 4 to 6 are those whom Christ calls His own. When Saul harried the church, the voice from heaven said, 'why do you persecute Me?' Acts 9:4. The one who is their shelter is also their fellow sufferer.

And the last verse, 'Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion,' finds its answer in the person the angel named, 'because He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21, and in the Zion to which believers have come, Hebrews 12:22-24. The longing that ends the psalm is the longing that Simeon, who was waiting for the consolation of Israel, held in his arms, Luke 2:25-30.

A caution: Psalm 14 is not a prophecy in which Christ speaks. Its link to Him is through what it diagnoses and what it hopes for. To make more of it than that would be to read into the psalm what the apostles did not.
study.god:
Psalm 14 shows God first as a watcher. 'The LORD looks down from heaven upon the sons of men to see if any understand, if any seek God.' Nothing escapes this gaze, and the fool's private thought in verse 1, spoken 'in his heart', is exactly what God sees. The irony of the psalm is that the man who says there is no God is being observed by Him as he says it. The God who is absent from the fool's reckoning is the God who knows the fool's heart, as Psalm 33:13-14 says, 'The LORD looks down from heaven; He sees all the sons of men.'

He is a God who searches to find, and He is patient enough to look before He judges. In Genesis 6:12 He looks at the earth and sees corruption; in Genesis 11:5 He comes down to see. The psalm's 'if any' is not a sign of doubt on God's part, since He knows the answer, but a way of showing that the verdict is reached after inspection, not by rumour. His judgement, when it comes, is just because it is informed.

He is holy, and holiness is dreadful to those who work iniquity. Verse 5 speaks of a sudden fear falling on the oppressors, 'for God is in the company of the righteous.' The presence that comforts one group terrifies the other. The same presence that is 'the LORD of Hosts is with us,' Psalm 46:7, is a fear to those who set themselves against His people.

He is on the side of the oppressed. The psalm says He is their shelter, and Psalm 12:5 sounds the same note: 'For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise.' God is not neutral about injustice, and the psalm holds that His taking of sides is an expression of His character, not of partiality.

He is faithful to His covenant. The name 'the LORD' appears four times in this psalm, the name by which He bound Himself to Israel. Even when He finds no one who seeks Him, His response is not to abandon the project but to bring salvation from Zion, as the last verse hopes. Isaiah says of a similar moment, 'His own arm brought salvation,' Isaiah 59:16. Where humanity cannot save itself, God acts.

The psalm also holds a tension without resolving it. It says that God is present among the righteous and that there is no one who does good. The reconciliation is grace: the righteous are those who take refuge in Him, and He makes them so, as Paul explains in Romans 3:24, 'and are justified freely by His grace.'

For worship, the psalm teaches humility and hope together. We approach God as those who have been found out and yet found by Him. To pray verse 7 is to admit that we cannot rescue ourselves, and to ask the God who sees to be the God who saves.

crossReferences.note: The near twin of Psalm 14. It speaks of 'God' where Psalm 14 has 'the LORD,' and in verse 5 it says God 'has scattered the bones of those who besieged you.' Reading the two together shows how the same poem could be sung with a national and a personal emphasis.

Paul's chain of quotations begins with Psalm 14:1-3 and adds lines from other psalms and Isaiah. He uses it to prove that Jews and Gentiles are 'all under sin,' so that no one can boast, and so that the righteousness given through faith in Christ, verse 22, is seen to be needed.

Before the flood God looked at the earth and 'saw that it was corrupt.' Psalm 14:2-3 uses the same word and the same act of looking. The psalm treats the human condition after the fall as a constant, not just a feature of the age of Noah.

'Then the LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of men were building.' The phrase 'sons of men' and the divine inspection come together in Psalm 14:2. The LORD looks down from heaven in the psalm and comes down in the story.

Abigail says of her husband, 'His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him.' It shows what the Hebrew word nabal meant in David's own experience: a person whose life shows contempt for accountability, not merely a man who lacks intellect.

'In his pride the wicked man does not seek Him; in all his schemes there is no God.' This is the fool of Psalm 14:1 seen from the inside. The atheism in question is a matter of pride and planning, not of argument.

The LORD looks and finds no one to intercede, 'So His own arm brought salvation.' It follows the same pattern as Psalm 14: God searches, finds no one, and then acts Himself. Verse 20, which promises a Redeemer for Zion, is echoed in Romans 11:26.

'For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise,' says the LORD. It answers the complaint of Psalm 14:4-6 in advance, and it shows God's vow to take up the cause of those who are devoured.

'Such is the generation of those who seek Him.' It uses the same verb as Psalm 14:2, where no one is found seeking. Psalm 24 speaks of a people that does seek, which is the fruit of God's work in them.

The turn after the diagnosis. 'But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed.' Paul offers, in place of the search that found no one, a righteousness given by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

'You have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God.' The salvation that Psalm 14:7 longs for from Zion is described as a place the church has already reached in Christ, with Jesus as mediator of a new covenant.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 14 belongs to the story right after the fall. Genesis 3 explains how sin entered, and the chapters that follow trace how quickly it spreads: a brother killed, a world filled with violence, God looking at the earth and seeing it 'corrupt', Genesis 6:12. Psalm 14 states what those chapters show, that when God looks at the human race He finds no one who seeks Him. It is the Old Testament's compact summary of the whole problem the rest of the story must solve.

The psalm sets a limit on what the story can hope for. If no one seeks God, then no reform from within will do. The Law given at Sinai shows what God requires but, as Paul says, 'the law merely brings awareness of sin,' Romans 3:20. The prophets keep calling the people back and keep finding that the powerful still 'devour my people,' Micah 3:3. The story therefore has to move toward a salvation that arrives from outside, and Psalm 14:7 is its shortest prayer for one.

That prayer runs through the Bible. Israel's restoration from exile, the coming of the Redeemer to Zion in Isaiah 59:20, and the promises to David all belong to the answer. The story reaches its turning point in Jesus, who is the one person of whom it is not true that He does no good. He comes 'to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10, takes the verdict of the psalm on Himself, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and by His resurrection opens a righteousness given by faith to Jews and Gentiles alike, Romans 3:21-26. Those who once belonged to the psalm's 'sons of men' now belong to the company of the righteous, and the God who found no one seeking Him has become the one who was found by those who did not seek, as Paul says in quoting Isaiah, 'I was found by those who did not seek Me,' Romans 10:20.

The end of the story fulfils the last verse. Believers have come already to Mount Zion, and the day is coming when God dwells with His people and the oppressor is no more, Revelation 21:3-4. On that day the psalm's 'Jacob' and 'Israel' rejoice, along with those from every nation, and the fool's 'There is no God' is answered by the sight of the LORD Himself.

quiz.q: What does the fool's denial of God in verse 1 primarily describe?

options.text: A practical, heart level rejection of God lived out in corrupt action, not merely an intellectual argument.
options.note: The nabal denies God in his heart and then acts corruptly, showing this is a matter of the will as much as the mind.

options.text: A carefully reasoned philosophical case against God's existence.
options.note: The psalm presents the denial as a heart posture that produces corrupt action, not a formal philosophical argument.

options.text: A momentary doubt quickly resolved by prayer.
options.note: The psalm describes settled corruption, not a fleeting doubt.

options.text: A rare condition limited to only a few individuals.
options.note: Verses 2-3 broaden this to describe humanity as a whole apart from grace, not merely a rare few.

quiz.q: How does Paul use this psalm in Romans 3?

options.text: He quotes it as scriptural proof that all people, apart from grace, are corrupt and none is righteous.
options.note: Romans 3:10-12 draws directly on this psalm's language to build the case for universal sinfulness.

options.text: He cites it to prove that only Gentiles are sinful.
options.note: Paul's argument in Romans 3 explicitly includes Jew and Gentile alike, not Gentiles only.

options.text: He uses it to argue that good works alone can restore a person to righteousness.
options.note: Paul's point is the opposite, that righteousness comes by faith, not works, precisely because none does good on their own.

options.text: He references it only in passing with no theological weight.
options.note: This understates its role; Paul builds a central part of his argument on this psalm's verdict.

quiz.q: What is the LORD described as for the oppressed in verse 6?

options.text: Their shelter, machaseh, even while sinners frustrate their plans.
options.note: The psalm insists God remains a true refuge for the righteous despite ongoing oppression.

options.text: Their judge who condemns them alongside the wicked.
options.note: The oppressed are distinguished from the wicked and are shown God's protection, not condemnation.

options.text: A distant observer with no active care for their situation.
options.note: The text actively names God as their shelter, not a distant or uninvolved figure.

options.text: Their eventual replacement by human rescuers.
options.note: This misses the direct point that God Himself, not a human substitute, is named as their shelter.

quiz.q: What does the psalm long for in its final verse?

options.text: That salvation would come from Zion and God would restore His captive people to rejoicing.
options.note: Verse 7 closes with this longing hope for restoration and joy.

options.text: That the fools would simply be ignored rather than judged.
options.note: The psalm's hope is restorative and salvific, not merely an appeal to ignore wrongdoing.

options.text: That Israel would gain military dominance over surrounding nations.
options.note: The text speaks of salvation and restoration from captivity, not a call to military conquest.

options.text: That the psalmist alone would be personally rescued from his enemies.
options.note: The hope in verse 7 is corporate, for Israel and Jacob as a whole, not merely for the psalmist individually.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's closing hope connect to Christ?

options.text: The salvation longed for from Zion is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, who brings the righteousness and restoration this psalm could only anticipate.
options.note: Paul's use of the psalm's diagnosis in Romans 3 sets up exactly this need, met fully in Christ's righteousness given by faith.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of Jerusalem's future rebuilding.
options.note: The psalm expresses a theological and spiritual longing, not a specific date for rebuilding.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the New Testament's teaching.
options.note: Paul's direct quotation of this psalm in Romans 3 shows a strong, explicit New Testament connection.

options.text: It refers only to a political restoration with no spiritual significance.
options.note: This understates the psalm's deeper spiritual longing for salvation, which the New Testament reads as fulfilled in Christ.

questions: The fool's denial of God happens quietly, in his heart, before it shows up in corrupt action. Where might practical unbelief, living as though God does not see or matter, be shaping your own choices?

Paul uses this psalm to say none of us is righteous on our own. How does it change your posture toward God and others when you accept this diagnosis honestly rather than comparing yourself favorably to 'worse' sinners?
The oppressed in this psalm have the LORD as their shelter even while their plans are frustrated. Where do you need to trust God as your refuge even though your circumstances have not yet improved?
The psalm ends with longing rather than resolution, 'oh, that salvation would come'. What are you still longing for God to complete or restore in your own life or community?

Salvation finally came from Zion in the person of Jesus. How does knowing that this psalm's hope has already been answered in Christ shape the way you pray for the needs and injustices you still see around you?

translationNotes.note: Fool renders nabal, describing moral and spiritual senselessness rather than mere intellectual deficiency; the denial is a heart posture, not primarily a philosophical claim.
This psalm is nearly identical to Psalm 53, with small differences in wording and in the divine name used, likely reflecting use in two different liturgical settings.
Salvation renders yeshuah, the same root later given as the personal name Jesus, linking this psalm's closing hope to its ultimate New Testament fulfillment.
